title: Science and Scientists of Medieval India
summary: In the medieval period science developed in two ways: continuing earlier traditions and absorbing Islamic and European influences. Traditional classical learning had received a setback; the Arab pattern of education was adopted and maktabs and madrasas came up with royal patronage and a set curriculum. Sheikh Abdullah and Sheikh Azizullah, specialists in rational science, headed madrasas at Sambhal and Agra; scholars from Arabia, Persia and Central Asia were invited. Primary school courses were reformed to include arithmetic, mensuration, geometry, astronomy, accountancy, public administration and agriculture; Akbar ordered mathematics to be taught. Karkhanas (large workshops) supplied provisions and equipment to the royal household and government departments and also served as centres of technical and vocational training; trained artisans later set up independent karkhanas.

Mathematics: Narayana Pandit (son of Narsimha Daivajna) – Ganitakaumudi and Bijaganitavatamsa; Gangadhara of Gujarat – Lilavati Karmadipika, Siddhantadipika and Lilavati Vyakhya (trigonometry: sine, cosine, tangent, cotangent); Nilakantha Somasutvan – Tantrasangraha; Ganesa Daivajna – Buddhivilasini (commentary on Lilavati); Krishna – Navankura on Bhaskara II's Bijaganita; Nilakantha Jyotirvida – Tajik (with many Persian technical terms); Faizi translated Bhaskara's Bijaganita for Akbar; Nasiruddin Tusi. Biology: Hamsadeva's Mrigapakshishastra (13th century) on animals and birds; Babur and Akbar studied it; Akbar bred elephants and horses; Jahangir in the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri described about 36 species of animals and was interested in plants (court artists drew about 57 plants); Mansur painted animals. Chemistry: paper-making – centres Kashmir, Sialkot, Zafarabad, Patna, Murshidabad, Ahmedabad, Aurangabad and Mysore; gunpowder – the Mughals knew it; Sukraniti (attributed to Sukracharya) describes preparing gunpowder from saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal in different ratios; fireworks; the Ain-i-Akbari mentions Akbar's perfume office; attar of roses is supposed to have been discovered by Nurjahan.

Astronomy: many commentaries; Mahendra Suri, court astronomer of Firoz Shah, developed the instrument Yantraraja; Parameshvara and Mahabhaskariya families of Kerala were famous astronomers and almanac-makers; Nilakantha Somasutvan commented on the Aryabhatiya; Kamalakara studied Islamic astronomy; Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II of Jaipur set up five observatories at Delhi, Ujjain, Varanasi, Mathura and Jaipur. Medicine: Ayurveda progressed slowly for lack of royal patronage but works compiled: Sarangadhara Samhita (13th century; uses opium and urine examination), Chikitsasangraha of Vangasena, Yogaratnakara and Bhavaprakasha of Bhavamishra; the Rasachikitsa (Rasashastra) system dealt with mineral medicines, mercurial and non-mercurial; the Siddha system of Tamil Nadu is attributed to the Siddhas with life-prolonging compositions; Unani Tibb came with Muslims about the 11th century: Ali-bin-Rabban's Firdausu-Hikmat summarised Greek and Indian medicine; Hakim Diya Muhammad's Majiny-e-Diyae; Firoz Shah's Tibb-i-Firozshahi; Tibbi Aurangzebi; Nuruddin Muhammad's Mualajat-i-Dara Shikohi. Agriculture: wheat, rice, barley, millets, pulses, oilseeds, cotton, sugarcane, indigo; Western Ghats pepper, Kashmir saffron, ginger and cinnamon from Tamil Nadu, cardamom, sandalwood and coconut from Kerala; tobacco, chillies, potato, guava, custard apple, cashew and pineapple introduced in the 16th–17th centuries; opium in Malwa and Bihar; mango grafting introduced by the Jesuits of Goa in the mid-16th century; Mughal gardens; irrigation by wells, tanks, canals, rahat, charas and dhenkli, and the Persian wheel in Agra; land measurement and classification by the State.

(a) Sarangadhara Samhita and Bhavaprakasha (Chikitsasangraha). (b) Use of opium in materia medica and urine examination for diagnosis.

vsa: Why was Rasachikitsa a unique system of medicine?
It was a system of mineral medicines – mercurial and non-mercurial preparations – and the Siddhas used it for life-prolonging compositions.
What were the two main functions of karkhanas?
They were manufacturing agencies supplying the royal household and government departments, and centres of technical and vocational training for young artisans.
Who were the Parameshvara and Mahabhaskariya families?
Famous families of astronomers and almanac-makers of Kerala.
Name any two Persian medical works of the medieval period.
Tibb-i-Firozshahi, Tibbi Aurangzebi, Majiny-e-Diyae and Mualajat-i-Dara Shikohi.
How was gunpowder prepared according to Sukraniti?
From saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal in different ratios for different types of guns.
What changes did medieval rulers make in primary school education?
They added arithmetic, mensuration, geometry, astronomy, accountancy, public administration and agriculture; Akbar made mathematics compulsory.
Name any two crops introduced during the medieval period.
Tobacco, chillies, potato, guava, custard apple, cashew, pineapple (any two).
What was the contribution of Jahangir in the field of biology?
In the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri he described about 36 species of animals and his court artists such as Mansur drew animals and about 57 plants accurately.
sa: Discuss the developments in the field of medicine in medieval India.

Ayurveda progressed slowly because of lack of patronage, but Sarangadhara Samhita (use of opium, urine examination), Chikitsasangraha, Yogaratnakara and Bhavaprakasha were compiled. Rasachikitsa and Siddha used mineral medicines. The Unani Tibb system came with Muslims and works like Firdausu-Hikmat, Majiny-e-Diyae, Tibb-i-Firozshahi and Mualajat-i-Dara Shikohi combined Greek, Arabic, Persian and Ayurvedic knowledge.
Write about astronomy in medieval India.

Commentaries on established ideas appeared; Mahendra Suri of Firoz Shah's court developed the Yantraraja; the Parameshvara and Mahabhaskariya families of Kerala were famous; Nilakantha Somasutvan commented on the Aryabhatiya; Kamalakara studied Islamic astronomy; Sawai Jai Singh II built observatories at Delhi, Ujjain, Varanasi, Mathura and Jaipur.
Describe agriculture in the medieval period.

The pattern was similar to early India, with wheat, rice, barley, millets, pulses, oilseeds, cotton, sugarcane and indigo; new crops (tobacco, chillies, potato, guava, cashew, pineapple) came in the 16th–17th centuries; mango grafting was introduced by the Jesuits; irrigation by wells, tanks, canals, rahat, charas and the Persian wheel; the State introduced land measurement and classification.
Write about mathematics in medieval India.

Narayana Pandit wrote Ganitakaumudi, Gangadhara the Lilavati Vyakhya, Nilakantha Somasutvan the Tantrasangraha, Ganesa Daivajna the Buddhivilasini; Faizi translated Bhaskara's Bijaganita; rules of trigonometry were given; Akbar made mathematics a subject of study.
Explain the use of chemistry in paper-making and gunpowder.

Paper-making spread across Kashmir, Sialkot, Patna, Ahmedabad, Mysore and other centres with similar methods; the Mughals used gunpowder in gunnery, and Sukraniti gives ratios of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal; fireworks and perfumes (attar of roses) were also developed.
la: Describe the education system and developments of science in the medieval period.

The Arab pattern of education led to maktabs and madrasas under royal patronage with a set curriculum; scholars from Arabia, Persia and Central Asia were invited; primary courses included arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, accountancy and agriculture. Karkhanas trained artisans. Works were produced in mathematics (Narayana Pandit, Gangadhara), biology (Hamsadeva, Jahangir), chemistry (paper, gunpowder), astronomy (Mahendra Suri, Jai Singh), medicine (Ayurveda and Unani) and agriculture (new crops), mostly commentaries; texts were translated between Sanskrit and Persian/Arabic.
Write an essay on science and scientists in the medieval period.

Science continued earlier traditions and took Islamic and European influences. Mathematicians: Narayana Pandit, Gangadhara, Nilakantha, Ganesa Daivajna, Faizi. Biology: Hamsadeva and Jahangir. Chemistry: paper, gunpowder (Sukraniti), perfumes. Astronomy: Mahendra Suri, Kerala families, Sawai Jai Singh II's five observatories. Medicine: Ayurveda, Rasa, Siddha and Unani. Agriculture: new crops, grafting and irrigation devices. Most works were commentaries.
Explain how irrigation was done and how agriculture developed in the medieval period.

Wells, tanks, canals, the rahat (Persian wheel), charas and dhenkli were used for irrigation; the Persian wheel was used near Agra. The State introduced a system of land measurement and classification, and new crops like tobacco, chillies, potato, guava, cashew and pineapple came in the 16th–17th centuries; opium was produced in Malwa and Bihar; Jesuits introduced mango grafting; Mughal gardens grew fruit trees.
